Hi Daniel — great to chat yesterday. Per our call, we want to align on realistic throughput commitments and the networking contours that matter for your VPC/on‑prem deployment. I took the liberty of attaching the workload CSV you shared and a first‑cut sizing workbook.

High level asks from our side so Marcus and Lauren can scope the recommendation:
- Confirm peak concurrent request mix (simple generations vs chat sessions with long KV cache).
- Expected 99th percentile token latency target (ms).
- Tolerance for cold‑start latency on model variant fallback.
- Any constraints on NIC configuration (SR‑IOV, jumbo frames, RDMA allowed?).

If you can drop the workloads and any perf test windows by EOD Friday we’ll return a sizing + deployment notes (network changes, MTU, storage recommendations) by Monday.

Thanks — Camila

Camila — thanks, sending answers inline and attaching our internal traffic export. Short answers first:
- Peak concurrent requests: 1,200 generation requests sustained over 5 minute windows; 2,400 short bursts for up to 90s during shift change syncs.
- Mix: ~60% single-pass generation (~250 tokens avg), 30% multi‑turn chat sessions (average 6 turns, where KV cache matters), 10% embeddings/rerank background jobs.
- 99th percentile latency target: 180ms token latency (app-level target for user-facing chat).
- Cold‑start tolerance: up to 2.5s for first token on a fallback model, preferably <800ms for primary variants.
- Network: SR‑IOV is available; we can enable jumbo frames; RDMA is not supported on our current nodes.

I'll attach infra export and the perf test windows. Let me know if you need anything else.

— Daniel
Daniel Park, Head of Infrastructure, Nimbus Health

Forwarding Daniel's replies. Key items to verify in sizing: 1. Sustained window of 1,200 concurrent gen requests (5 min) with frequent 2.5x bursts. 2. Primary latency SLO tight (180ms 99p). 3. SR‑IOV + jumbo frames available; no RDMA.

High priority engineering considerations for sizing table:
- How many inference workers per GPU given average sequence length distribution and KV cache hit rates?
- Expected token/sec per GPU for their target SLO (we should also show conservative and optimistic numbers).
- Network egress per GPU when KV cache misses/refresh occur (we need headroom for cache refill storms).
- Warmup strategy: prefer persistent warm VMs vs ephemeral pool with proactive cache prewarming.

Marcus — can you sketch two runbooks: "Sustained‑optimized" (runs denser with aggressive batching + larger KV caches) and "Burst‑resilient" (more conservative batching but faster cold‑start recovery) and call out NIC tuning (MTU, tx queues) and expected failover windows? I want a one‑page summary to walk Daniel through on Thursday.

-Camila

From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
To: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 15 Feb 2028 09:08:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Fwd: Nimbus Health — on‑prem GPU headroom & networking review

Thanks — I sketched the two runbooks and a compact sizing math sheet (attached in our workbook). Summary below.

Sizing summary (ballpark numbers for Nimbus profile):
- Model profile: LLM-13B dense with KV cache characteristics (avg token/window 250, warm cache hit ≈ 78%).
- Sustained‑optimized: allocate 1 GPU per 48 concurrent light gens (250 token avg) → ~25 GPUs to cover 1,200 sustained with 25% safety headroom for maintenance and degradation. Optimistic throughput per A100‑class GPU: ~1,920 tokens/sec (with batch aggregation).
- Burst‑resilient: target lower packing, 1 GPU per 32 concurrent sessions → ~40 GPUs to absorb 2.4k short bursts with buffer capacity and faster fallbacks. Reserve an additional 6 GPUs for KV cache refill storm mitigation (prefetch lanes).
- Cold start behavior: with persistent warm workers, first token latency ≈ 350–600ms; with ephemeral workers (spinup) it jumps to 1.6–2.8s depending on image startup and model load time. Recommendation: hybrid pool — 60% warm persistent, 40% burstable ephemeral.

Network and deployment notes:
- NIC tuning: enable SR‑IOV, set MTU 9000, increase tx/rx queue sizes to avoid drops at 10Gbps+ bursts.
- NFS vs local scratch: use local NVMe for KV cache; put model artifacts on a read‑only NFS share during orchestrated rollout (to speed model swaps) but avoid run‑time KV traffic over NFS.
- Monitoring: instrument token/sec per GPU, queue depth, and cache hit metrics; alert at 70% sustained sustained token/sec and 85% GPU mem utilization.

Next steps: I’ll convert this to a one‑page summary and call out exact GPU SKUs we recommend (A100x2 / H100 variants) plus a migration playbook for swapping into warm pool. Target to share with Daniel Thursday morning.

— Marcus
Marcus Lin, Senior Infrastructure Architect, Redwood Inference
